title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 135 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 640–643 (Night 135, continuing directly from nights-134), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 135 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Disguised as a slave-girl, Tāj al-Mulūk is brought past the palace eunuch by the old nurse and reaches the Lady Dunyā, and for a month, then half a year, the two live together in secret. Meanwhile the vizier and ʿAzīz, giving him up for lost, ride home to his father, King Sulaymān Shāh, who raises an army and marches out to find his son. Tāj al-Mulūk tells Dunyā who he really is; but that night the lovers oversleep, the eunuch Kāfūr finds them together, and Dunyā's father, King Shahramān, condemns the prince to death. The night breaks off with the executioner's sword raised. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالثَّلٰثُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-thalāthūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the thirty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirty-fifth night,
sentences.n: The print spells thalāthūn without its long alif (والثلثون); the small alif over the lām is ours, to show the long vowel.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْحَاجِبَ قَالَ لِلْعَجُوزِ أَنَا لَا أَعْرِفُ جَارِيَةً وَلَا غَيْرَهَا وَلَا يَدْخُلُ أَحَدٌ حَتَّى أُفَتِّشَهُ كَمَا أَمَرَنِي الْمَلِكُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-ḥājiba qāla li-al-ʿajūzi anā lā aʿrifu jāriyatan wa-lā ghayrahā wa-lā yadkhulu aḥadun ḥattā ufattishahu kamā amaranī al-maliku
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the chamberlain said to the old woman: I do not know a slave-girl nor other-than-her; and no one enters until I search him, as the king commanded me.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the chamberlain said to the old woman, “Slave-girl or no slave-girl, it is all one to me: nobody goes in until I have searched them, as the king ordered me.”
sentences.n: The night takes up the scene where the last one broke off: the old nurse is bringing Tāj al-Mulūk into the palace dressed as a slave-girl, and the eunuch at the gate wants to search “her”. The man is called al-ḥājib, “the chamberlain”, here, and al-khādim, “the eunuch, the servant”, a few lines on. lā aʿrifu jāriyatan wa-lā ghayrahā, “I know no slave-girl nor anyone else”: I make no exceptions.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ الْعَجُوزُ وَقَدْ أَظْهَرَتِ الْغَضَبَ أَنَا أَعْرِفُ أَنَّكَ عَاقِلٌ وَمُؤَدَّبٌ فَإِنْ كَانَ حَالُكَ قَدْ تَغَيَّرَ فَإِنِّي أُعْلِمُهَا بِذٰلِكَ وَأُخْبِرُهَا أَنَّكَ تَعَرَّضْتَ لِجَارِيَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu al-ʿajūzu wa-qad aẓharati al-ghaḍaba anā aʿrifu annaka ʿāqilun wa-muʾaddabun fa-in kāna ḥāluka qad taghayyara fa-innī uʿlimuhā bi-dhālika wa-ukhbiruhā annaka taʿarraḍta li-jāriyatihā
sentences.l: So the old woman said to him, and she had made-show-of anger: I know that you are sensible and well-mannered; so if your state has changed, then I shall let-her-know of that and tell her that you interfered with her slave-girl.
sentences.i: The old woman put on a show of anger and said to him, “I have always known you for a sensible, well-bred man. But if you have changed, I shall let her know it, and tell her that you laid hands on her slave-girl.”
sentences.n: “Her” is the Lady Dunyā, the king's daughter, whose servant the nurse is. taʿarraḍa li-, “to accost, to meddle with”: li- marks the one interfered with. The print marks the doubled letters of muʾaddab, taghayyara and taʿarraḍta.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ زَعَقَتْ عَلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ اعْبُرِي يَا جَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma zaʿaqat ʿalā tāji al-mulūki wa-qālat lahu uʿburī yā jāriyatu
sentences.l: Then she shouted at Tāj al-Mulūk and said to him: Pass (fem.), O slave-girl!
sentences.i: Then she shouted at Tāj al-Mulūk, “Go on in, girl!”
sentences.n: zaʿaqa ʿalā, “to shout at”, a word of the spoken language. The imperative ʿburī is feminine: she keeps up the disguise, though the narrator says lahu, “to him”.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ عَبَرَ إِلَى دَاخِلِ الدِّهْلِيزِ كَمَا أَمَرَتْهُ وَسَكَتَ الْخَادِمُ وَلَمْ يَتَكَلَّمْ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika ʿabara ilā dākhili al-dihlīzi kamā amarathu wa-sakata al-khādimu wa-lam yatakallam
sentences.l: So at that he passed to the inside of the vestibule as she commanded him, and the eunuch was silent and did not speak.
sentences.i: At that he went on into the passage as she had told him, and the eunuch held his tongue and said nothing.
sentences.n: dihlīz, “vestibule, entrance passage”, a Persian loanword. The print marks the doubled lām of yatakallam.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ تَاجَ الْمُلُوكِ عَدَّ خَمْسَةَ أَبْوَابٍ وَدَخَلَ الْبَابَ السَّادِسَ فَوَجَدَ السَّيِّدَةَ دُنْيَا وَاقِفَةً فِي انْتِظَارِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna tāja al-mulūki ʿadda khamsata abwābin wa-dakhala al-bāba al-sādisa fa-wajada al-sayyidata dunyā wāqifatan fī intiẓārihā
sentences.l: Then Tāj al-Mulūk counted five doors and entered the sixth door, and found the Lady Dunyā standing in awaiting-her.
sentences.i: Then Tāj al-Mulūk counted five doors and went in at the sixth, and there was the Lady Dunyā, standing and waiting for her.
sentences.n: fī intiẓārihā, “in waiting for her”: the feminine is the slave-girl Dunyā has been told to expect. The nurse had given him the count of the doors beforehand.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ عَرَفَتْهُ فَضَمَّتْهُ إِلَى صَدْرِهَا وَضَمَّهَا إِلَى صَدْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu ʿarafathu fa-ḍammathu ilā ṣadrihā wa-ḍammahā ilā ṣadrihi
sentences.l: And when she saw him, she knew him, and she pressed him to her breast and he pressed her to his breast.
sentences.i: When she saw him she knew him, and she clasped him to her breast, and he clasped her to his.
sentences.n: The print has نضمته, a misprint for faḍammathu (فضمته), “and she pressed him”, corrected here. The print marks the doubled mīm of ḍammahā.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَخَلَتِ الْعَجُوزُ عَلَيْهِمَا وَتَحَيَّلَتْ عَلَى صَرْفِ الْجَوَارِي خَوْفًا مِنَ الْفَضِيحَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma dakhalati al-ʿajūzu ʿalayhimā wa-taḥayyalat ʿalā ṣarfi al-jawārī khawfan mina al-faḍīḥati
sentences.l: Then the old woman came in upon the two of them and used-a-ruse for sending-away the slave-girls, for fear of the scandal.
sentences.i: Then the old woman came in to them and found a way to get the slave-girls out of the room, for fear of discovery.
sentences.n: taḥayyala ʿalā, “to contrive, to find a trick for”; the print marks its doubled yāʾ.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتِ السَّيِّدَةُ دُنْيَا لِلْعَجُوزِكُونِي أَنْتِ بَوَّابَةً
sentences.tr: thumma qālati al-sayyidatu dunyā li-al-ʿajūzi kūnī anti bawwābatan
sentences.l: Then the Lady Dunyā said to the old woman: Be you a door-keeper (fem.).
sentences.i: Then the Lady Dunyā said to the old woman, “You keep the door.”
sentences.n: The print runs li-al-ʿajūzi, “to the old woman”, and kūnī, “be”, together (للعجوزكوني). It marks the doubled wāw of bawwāba.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ اخْتَلَتْ هِيَ وَتَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ وَلَمْ يَزَالَا فِي ضَمٍّ وَعِنٰقٍ وَالْتِفَافِ سَاقٍ عَلَى سَاقٍ إِلَى وَقْتِ السَّحَرِ
sentences.tr: thumma ikhtalat hiya wa-tāju al-mulūki wa-lam yazālā fī ḍammin wa-ʿināqin wa-iltifāfi sāqin ʿalā sāqin ilā waqti al-saḥari
sentences.l: Then she was-alone, she and Tāj al-Mulūk, and the two did not cease in pressing and embracing and the twining of leg upon leg, till the time of the before-dawn.
sentences.i: Then she and Tāj al-Mulūk were left alone together, and they lay embracing and clasped, leg twined with leg, until the hour before dawn.
sentences.n: ikhtalā, “to be alone, in private”. ḍamm wa-ʿināq wa-iltifāf al-sāq ʿalā al-sāq, “pressing, embracing and the twining of leg on leg”, is a stock phrase of the Nights for lovers in bed. The print spells ʿināq with a small alif over the nūn (عنٰق) in place of the alif letter.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرُبَ الصَّبَاحُ خَرَجَتْ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَأَغْلَقَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْبَابَ وَدَخَلَتْ مَقْصُورَةً أُخْرَى وَجَلَسَتْ عَلَى جَرْيِ عَادَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaruba al-ṣabāḥu kharajat min ʿindihi wa-aghlaqat ʿalayhi al-bāba wa-dakhalat maqṣūratan ukhrā wa-jalasat ʿalā jaryi ʿādatihā
sentences.l: And when the morning drew near, she went out from beside him and locked the door upon him, and entered another chamber and sat according to the running of her custom.
sentences.i: As morning came near she left him, locked the door on him, went into another room and sat there as she always did.
sentences.n: maqṣūra, “a private chamber”, the women's apartment. ʿalā jarī ʿādatihā, “on the running of her habit”: “as usual”.

sentences.t: وَأَتَتْ إِلَيْهَا الْجَوَارِي فَقَضَتْ حَوَائِجَهُنَّ وَصَارَتْ تُحَدِّثُهُنَّ
sentences.tr: wa-atat ilayhā al-jawārī fa-qaḍat ḥawāʾijahunna wa-ṣārat tuḥaddithuhunna
sentences.l: And the slave-girls came to her, and she settled their needs, and began to talk with them.
sentences.i: The slave-girls came to her, and she saw to what they needed and chatted with them.
sentences.n: ṣāra with a present verb, “to begin to (do)”, a usage of later Arabic.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِلْجَوَارِي اخْرُجْنَ الْآنَ مِنْ عِنْدِي فَإِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَنْشَرِحَ وَحْدِي
sentences.tr: thumma qālat li-al-jawārī ukhrujna al-āna min ʿindī fa-innī urīdu an anshariḥa waḥdī
sentences.l: Then she said to the slave-girls: Go out (fem. pl.) now from beside me, for I want to be-at-ease alone.
sentences.i: Then she said to the slave-girls, “Leave me now; I want to be on my own and take my ease.”
sentences.n: inshiraḥ, literally “expansion (of the breast)”, is cheerfulness and ease; here, to relax by herself.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجَتِ الْجَوَارِي مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَأَتَتْ إِلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajati al-jawārī min ʿindihā wa-atat ilā tāji al-mulūki
sentences.l: So the slave-girls went out from beside her, and she came to Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.i: So the slave-girls left her, and she went back to Tāj al-Mulūk.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَتَتْ إِلَيْهِمَا الْعَجُوزُ وَمَعَهَا شَيْءٌ مِنَ الْأَكْلِ فَأَكَلُوا وَأَخَذَا فِى الْهِرَاشِ إِلَى وَقْتِ السَّحَرِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā atat ilayhimā al-ʿajūzu wa-maʿahā shayʾun mina al-akli fa-akalū wa-akhadhā fī al-hirāshi ilā waqti al-saḥari
sentences.l: Then she — there came to the two of them the old woman, and with her something of the food, and they ate; and the two took to the sporting until the time of the before-dawn.
sentences.i: Then the old woman came to them with something to eat, and they ate, and the two of them fell to their love-play until the hour before dawn.
sentences.n: thumma innahā, “then she”: a pronoun announcing the subject, which follows only after the verb, al-ʿajūz; a loose construction common in the Nights. hirāsh, properly “wrangling, scuffling”, is used in the Nights of lovers' play. The print spells fī with a final ى (فى).

sentences.t: فَأَغْلَقَتْ عَلَيْهِمَا الْبَابَ مِثْلَ الْيَوْمِ الْأَوَّلِ وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا عَلَى ذٰلِكَ مُدَّةَ شَهْرٍ كَامِلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-aghlaqat ʿalayhimā al-bāba mithla al-yawmi al-awwali wa-lam yazālū ʿalā dhālika muddata shahrin kāmilin
sentences.l: And she locked the door upon the two of them like the first day, and they did not cease upon that for the space of a whole month.
sentences.i: Then she locked the door on them as on the first day; and so they went on for a whole month.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَالسَّيِّدَةِ دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri tāji al-mulūki wa-al-sayyidati dunyā
sentences.l: This is what was of the affair of Tāj al-Mulūk and the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.i: So much for Tāj al-Mulūk and the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.n: The storyteller's formula for leaving one thread of the plot and taking up another.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْوَزِيرِ وَعَزِيزٍ فَإِنَّهُمَا لَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ إِلَى قَصْرِ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ وَمَكَثَ تِلْكَ الْمُدَّةَ عَلِمَا أَنَّهُ لَا يَخْرُجُ مِنْهُ أَبَداً وَأَنَّهُ هَالِكٌ لَا مَحَالَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-wazīri wa-ʿazīzin fa-innahumā lammā tawajjaha tāju al-mulūki ilā qaṣri binti al-maliki wa-makatha tilka al-muddata ʿalimā annahu lā yakhruju minhu abadan wa-annahu hālikun lā maḥālata
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of the vizier and ʿAzīz, the two of them, when Tāj al-Mulūk went to the palace of the king's daughter and stayed that space, knew that he would not come out of it ever, and that he was perishing, no escaping it.
sentences.i: As for the vizier and ʿAzīz: when Tāj al-Mulūk had gone into the king's daughter's palace and stayed there all that time, they were sure he would never come out of it and was certainly a dead man.
sentences.n: fa-innahumā … ʿalimā, “as for the two of them … they knew”: the sentence starts with them, breaks off for the lammā clause, and comes back to them. lā maḥālata, “there is no avoiding it”: “certainly”. The vizier is Tāj al-Mulūk's father's vizier, sent with him; ʿAzīz is the young man whose own story he heard. The print sets the tanwīn of abadan over the final alif.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ عَزِيزٌ لِلْوَزِيرِ يَا وَالِدِي مَا ذَا تَصْنَعُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ʿazīzun li-al-wazīri yā wālidī mā dhā taṣnaʿu
sentences.l: And ʿAzīz said to the vizier: O my father, what is it you will do?
sentences.i: ʿAzīz said to the vizier, “Father, what will you do?”
sentences.n: yā wālidī, “my father”: a respectful address to an older man. The print writes mā dhā as two words.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْوَزِيرُ يَا وَلَدِي إِنَّ هٰذَا الْأَمْرَ مُشْكِلٌ وَإِنْ لَمْ نَرْجِعْ إِلَى أَبِيهِ وَنُعْلِمْهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَلُومُنَا عَلَى ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-wazīru yā waladī inna hādhā al-amra mushkilun wa-in lam narjiʿ ilā abīhi wa-nuʿlimhu fa-innahu yalūmunā ʿalā dhālika
sentences.l: And the vizier said: O my son, this matter is difficult; and if we do not return to his father and let-him-know, he will blame us for that.
sentences.i: The vizier said, “My son, this is a hard case. But if we do not go back to his father and tell him, he will blame us for it.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَجَهَّزَا فِى الْوَقْتِ وَالسَّاعَةِ وَتَوَجَّهَا إِلَى الْأَرْضِ الْخَضْرَاءِ وَالْعَمُودَيْنِ وَتَحْتَ الْمَلِكِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ
sentences.tr: thumma tajahhazā fī al-waqti wa-al-sāʿati wa-tawajjahā ilā al-arḍi al-khaḍrāʾi wa-al-ʿamūdayni wa-taḥta al-maliki sulaymāna shāh
sentences.l: Then the two made-ready in the time and the hour and headed to the Green Land and the Two Pillars, and under King Sulaymān Shāh.
sentences.i: Then they made ready there and then, and set out for the Green Land and the Two Pillars, the realm of King Sulaymān Shāh.
sentences.n: fī al-waqti wa-al-sāʿati, “in the time and the hour”: at once. The Green Land and the Two Pillars is Sulaymān Shāh's kingdom, Tāj al-Mulūk's home. wa-taḥta al-malik, “and under the king”, is strained, and we are not sure of it; it may be a misprint for wa-takhti al-maliki (وتخت), “and the throne(-seat) of King Sulaymān Shāh”. The print's reading is kept, and taken as “(the land) under King Sulaymān Shāh”. The print marks the doubled letters of tajahhazā and tawajjahā.

sentences.t: وَسَارَا يَقْطَعَانِ الْأَوْدِيَةَ فِى اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَا عَلَى الْمَلِكِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ وَأَخْبَرَاهُ بِمَا جَرَى لِوَلَدِهِ وَأَنَّهُ مِنْ حِينِ دَخَلَ قَصْرَ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ لَمْ يَعْلَمُوا لَهُ خَبَرًا
sentences.tr: wa-sārā yaqṭaʿāni al-awdiyata fī al-layli wa-al-nahāri ilā an dakhalā ʿalā al-maliki sulaymāna shāh wa-akhbarāhu bi-mā jarā li-waladihi wa-annahu min ḥīni dakhala qaṣra binti al-maliki lam yaʿlamū lahu khabaran
sentences.l: And the two journeyed, cutting the valleys in the night and the day, until they came in upon King Sulaymān Shāh and told him of what had befallen his son, and that since the moment he entered the palace of the king's daughter they had not known any news of him.
sentences.i: They travelled night and day, crossing valley after valley, until they came before King Sulaymān Shāh and told him what had happened to his son: that since he went into the princess's palace they had heard nothing of him.
sentences.n: The print has الى ن, a misprint for ilā an (الى ان), “until”, corrected here. akhbara bi-, “to inform of”: the verb takes bi-. lam yaʿlamū, “they did not know”, is plural where the two travellers would call for the dual; Middle Arabic often lets the plural stand for two.

sentences.t: فَعِنْدَ ذٰلِكَ قَامَتْ عَلَيْهِ الْقِيَامَةُ وَاشْتَدَّ بِهِ النَّدَامَةُ
sentences.tr: fa-ʿinda dhālika qāmat ʿalayhi al-qiyāmatu wa-ishtadda bihi al-nadāmatu
sentences.l: So at that the Resurrection rose upon him, and the regret grew-hard upon him.
sentences.i: At that it was as if the Day of Judgement had come down on him, and he was overwhelmed with remorse.
sentences.n: qāmat ʿalayhi al-qiyāma, “the Resurrection rose upon him”: he was thrown into utter turmoil. ishtadda, “grew strong”, is masculine before the feminine nadāma, “regret”, a looseness the print allows; it marks the verb's doubled dāl.

sentences.t: وَأَمَرَأَنْ يُنَادَى فِي مَمْلَكَتِهِ بِالْجِهَادِ
sentences.tr: wa-amara an yunādā fī mamlakatihi bi-al-jihādi
sentences.l: And he commanded that it be proclaimed in his kingdom for the holy-war.
sentences.i: He ordered that war be proclaimed throughout his kingdom.
sentences.n: The print runs amara, “he commanded”, and an, “that”, together (وامران). nādā bi-, “to proclaim, to cry out”: bi- marks what is announced. jihād here is simply a call to arms.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَرَّزَ الْعَسَاكِرَ إِلَى خَارِجِ مَدِينَتِهِ وَنَصَبَ لَهُمُ الْخِيَامَ وَجَلَسَ فِي سُرَادِقِهِ حَتَّى اجْتَمَعَتِ الْجُيُوشُ مِنْ سَائِرِ الْأَقْطَارِ
sentences.tr: thumma barraza al-ʿasākira ilā khāriji madīnatihi wa-naṣaba lahumu al-khiyāma wa-jalasa fī surādiqihi ḥattā ijtamaʿati al-juyūshu min sāʾiri al-aqṭāri
sentences.l: Then he brought-out the troops to the outside of his city, and pitched for them the tents, and sat in his pavilion until the armies gathered from all the regions.
sentences.i: Then he marched his troops out of the city, pitched tents for them, and sat in his pavilion until the armies had gathered from every quarter.
sentences.n: barraza, “to bring out (into the open)”, is our reading; the unpointed برز could also be baraza, “came out”, with al-ʿasākir, “the troops”, as its subject. surādiq, “a great tent, pavilion”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ رَعِيَّتُهُ تُحِبُّهُ لِكَثْرَةِ عَدْلِهِ وَإِحْسَانِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat raʿiyyatuhu tuḥibbuhu li-kathrati ʿadlihi wa-iḥsānihi
sentences.l: And his subjects used to love him for the abundance of his justice and his beneficence.
sentences.i: His people loved him, for he was just and generous above measure.
sentences.n: li-kathrati, “for the abundance of”: li- gives the reason.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَارَ فِي عَسْكَرٍ سَدَّ الْأُفُقَ مُتَوَجِّهًا فِي طَلَبِ وَلَدِةِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: thumma sāra fī ʿaskarin sadda al-ufuqa mutawajjihan fī ṭalabi waladihi tāji al-mulūki
sentences.l: Then he marched in an army that blocked the horizon, heading in search of his son Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.i: Then he set out at the head of an army that blotted out the horizon, going in search of his son Tāj al-Mulūk.
sentences.n: The print writes the pronoun of waladihi, “his son”, with a final tāʾ marbūṭa (ولدة), a habit of this edition; read -hi. It marks the doubled letters of sadda and mutawajjihan.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ هٰؤُلَاءِ
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amri hāʾulāʾi
sentences.l: This is what was of the affair of these.
sentences.i: So much for them.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَالسَّيِّدَةِ دُنْيَا فَإِنَّهُمَا أَقَامَا عَلَى حَالِهِمَا نِصْفَ سَنَةٍ وَهُمَا كُلَّ يَوْمٍ يَزْدَادَانِ مَحَبَّةً فِي بَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri tāji al-mulūki wa-al-sayyidati dunyā fa-innahumā aqāmā ʿalā ḥālihimā niṣfa sanatin wa-humā kulla yawmin yazdādāni maḥabbatan fī baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of Tāj al-Mulūk and the Lady Dunyā, the two of them remained upon their state half a year, and they, every day, increasing in love in each-other.
sentences.i: As for Tāj al-Mulūk and the Lady Dunyā, they went on as they were for half a year, and every day they loved each other more.
sentences.n: fī baʿḍihimā, “in each other”: Middle Arabic uses baʿḍ, “some, part”, for the reciprocal “each other”.

sentences.t: وَزَادَ عَلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ الْعِشْقُ وَالْهُيَامُ وَالْوَجْدُ وَالْغَرَامُ حَتَّى أَفْصَحَ لَهَا عَنِ الضَّمِيرِ
sentences.tr: wa-zāda ʿalā tāji al-mulūki al-ʿishqu wa-al-huyāmu wa-al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu ḥattā afṣaḥa lahā ʿani al-ḍamīri
sentences.l: And there grew upon Tāj al-Mulūk the passion and the love-madness and the longing and the ardour, until he made-plain to her about the inner-heart.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk's passion, his love-sickness, longing and desire grew on him, until he opened his heart to her.
sentences.n: The four nouns are near-synonyms for love, piled up as the Nights likes to: ʿishq, passionate love; huyām, love that drives one to wander distracted; wajd, longing; gharām, ardent desire. al-ḍamīr, “what is hidden within”, one's secret thoughts.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهَا اعْلَمِي يَا حَبِيبَةَ الْقَلْبِ وَالْفُؤَادِ أَنِّي كُلَّمَا أَقَمْتُ عِنْدَكِ اِزْدْدتُّ هُيَامًا وَوَجْدًا وَغَرَامًا لِأَنِّي مَا بَلَغْتُ الْمَرَامَ بِالْكُلِّيَّةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahā iʿlamī yā ḥabībata al-qalbi wa-al-fuʾādi annī kullamā aqamtu ʿindaki izdattu huyāman wa-wajdan wa-gharāman li-annī mā balaghtu al-marāma bi-al-kulliyyati
sentences.l: And he said to her: Know, O beloved of the heart and the inmost-heart, that whenever I stay with you, I increase in love-madness and longing and ardour, because I have not reached the goal in-the-entirety.
sentences.i: He said to her, “Beloved of my heart and soul, the longer I stay with you, the more I am mad with love, with longing and desire, because I have not yet had all that I want.”
sentences.n: The print points izdadtu, “I increased”, unusually: a sukūn on the first dāl and a doubled tāʾ (ازدْدتُّ), the second dāl being swallowed into the tāʾ as in speech (izdattu); the marks are kept as printed. bi-al-kulliyya, “in the whole”: entirely. What he has not reached, he explains in a moment, is not what Dunyā first supposes.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَهُ وَمَا تُرِيدُ يَا نُورَ عَيْنِي وَثَمَرَةَ فُؤَادِي إِنْ شِئْتَ غَيْرَ الضَّمِّ وَالْعِنَاقِ وَالْتِفَافِ السَّاقِ عَلَى السَّاقِ فَافْعَلِ الَّذِي يُرْضِيكَ وَلَيْسَ لِلّٰهِ فِينَا شَرِيكٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lahu wa-mā turīdu yā nūra ʿaynī wa-thamarata fuʾādī in shiʾta ghayra al-ḍammi wa-al-ʿināqi wa-iltifāfi al-sāqi ʿalā al-sāqi fa-ifʿali alladhī yurḍīka wa-laysa li-allāhi fīnā sharīkun
sentences.l: And she said to him: And what do you want, O light of my eye and fruit of my heart? If you wish other than the pressing and the embracing and the twining of the leg upon the leg, then do that which pleases you; and there is not to God in us a partner.
sentences.i: She said, “And what is it you want, light of my eyes, fruit of my heart? If you want more than holding and embracing and lying with your legs twined in mine, do whatever pleases you; and God has no rival in us.”
sentences.n: laysa li-allāhi fīnā sharīk, “God has no partner in us”: a play on the creed that God has no partner; she means that they two belong wholly to each other, with no third to share or forbid. li- marks the one to whom something belongs.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَيْسَ مُرَادِي هٰكَذَا وَإِنَّمَا مُرَادِي أَنْ أُخْبِرَكِ بِحَقِيقَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla laysa murādī hākadhā wa-innamā murādī an ukhbiraki bi-ḥaqīqatī
sentences.l: And he said: My desire is not thus; but rather my desire is that I tell you of my truth.
sentences.i: He said, “That is not what I mean. What I want is to tell you who I really am.”
sentences.n: akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: bi- marks the matter told. ḥaqīqa, “the truth (of a thing)”, here “who I truly am”.

sentences.t: فَاعْلَمِي أَنِّي لَسْتُ بِتَاجِرٍ بَلْ أَنَا مَلِكٌ ابْنُ مَلِكٍ
sentences.tr: fa-iʿlamī annī lastu bi-tājirin bal anā malikun ibnu malikin
sentences.l: So know that I am not a merchant; rather I am a king, son of a king.
sentences.i: “Know that I am no merchant. I am a king, and a king's son.”
sentences.n: lastu bi-tājirin: after laysa, bi- simply introduces the predicate, “not a merchant”, and adds emphasis.

sentences.t: وَاسْمُ أَبِي الْمَلِكُ الْأَعْظَمُ سُلَيْمَانُ شَاهْ الَّذِي أَنْفَذَ الْوَزِيرَ رَسُولًا إِلَى أَبِيكِ لِيَخْطُبَكِ لِي فَلَمَّا بَلَغَكِ الْخَبَرُ مَا رَضِيتِ
sentences.tr: wa-ismu abī al-maliku al-aʿẓamu sulaymānu shāh alladhī anfadha al-wazīra rasūlan ilā abīki li-yakhṭubaki lī fa-lammā balaghaki al-khabaru mā raḍīti
sentences.l: And the name of my father is the King the Greatest, Sulaymān Shāh, who sent the vizier as messenger to your father that he might ask-in-marriage you for me; and when the news reached you, you were not content.
sentences.i: “My father is the great king Sulaymān Shāh, who sent his vizier to your father as an envoy to ask for your hand for me; and when you heard of it, you would not have it.”
sentences.n: li-yakhṭubaki, “so that he might ask for you in marriage”: li- of purpose; lī, “for me”. The print itself marks the feminine endings in li-yakhṭubaki, balaghaki and raḍīti, to make clear he is speaking to a woman.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ قَصَّ عَلَيْهَا قِصَّتَهُ مِنَ الْأَوَّلِ إِلَى الْآخِرِ وَلَيْسَ فِى الْإِعَادَةِ إِفَادَةٌ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu qaṣṣa ʿalayhā qiṣṣatahu mina al-awwali ilā al-ākhiri wa-laysa fī al-iʿādati ifādatun
sentences.l: Then he related to her his story from the first to the last; and there is not in the repetition any profit.
sentences.i: Then he told her his whole story from beginning to end; but there is nothing to be gained by telling it again.
sentences.n: wa-laysa fī al-iʿādati ifāda, “there is no profit in repetition”: the storyteller's rhyming formula for skipping what the listener has already heard. The print marks the doubled ṣād of qaṣṣa.

sentences.t: وَأُرِيدُ الْآنَ أَنْ أَتَوَجَّهَ إِلَى أَبِي لِيُرْسِلَ رَسُولًا إِلَى أَبِيكِ وَيَخْطُبَكِ مِنْهُ وَنَسْتَرِيحَ
sentences.tr: wa-urīdu al-āna an atawajjaha ilā abī li-yursila rasūlan ilā abīki wa-yakhṭubaki minhu wa-nastarīḥa
sentences.l: And I want now to go to my father, that he may send a messenger to your father and ask-in-marriage you from him, and we be at rest.
sentences.i: “Now I want to go to my father, so that he can send an envoy to your father and ask him for your hand, and then we can be at peace.”
sentences.n: The sentence returns to Tāj al-Mulūk's own words after the narrator's aside. khaṭaba … min, “to ask for (a woman) from (her guardian)”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ ذٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ فَرِحَتْ فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا لِأَنَّهُ وَافَقَ غَرَضَهَا ثُمَّ بَاتَا عَلَى هٰذَا الِاتِّفَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat dhālika al-kalāma fariḥat faraḥan shadīdan li-annahu wāfaqa gharaḍahā thumma bātā ʿalā hādhā al-ittifāqi
sentences.l: And when she heard that speech, she rejoiced a strong rejoicing, because it agreed with her purpose; then the two passed-the-night upon this agreement.
sentences.i: When she heard this she was overjoyed, for it was just what she wanted; and they spent the night on that understanding.
sentences.n: The print has بانا, a misprint for bātā (باتا), “the two spent the night”, corrected here.

sentences.t: وَاتَّفَقَ بِالْأَمْرِ الْمُقَدَّرِ أَنَّ النَّوْمَ غَلَبَ عَلَيْهِمَا فِي تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّيَالِي وَاسْتَمَرَّا إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ
sentences.tr: wa-ittafaqa bi-al-amri al-muqaddari anna al-nawma ghalaba ʿalayhimā fī tilka al-laylati min dūni al-layālī wa-istamarrā ilā an ṭalaʿati al-shamsu
sentences.l: And it chanced, by the decreed matter, that the sleep overcame the two of them in that night, apart-from the nights, and they continued until the sun rose.
sentences.i: And as fate had decreed, that night of all nights sleep overcame them, and they slept on until the sun was up.
sentences.n: The print has وانفق, a misprint for wa-ittafaqa (واتفق), “and it happened”, corrected here. bi-al-amri al-muqaddar, “by the decreed affair”: bi- of cause, “as fate would have it”. min dūni al-layālī, “to the exclusion of the (other) nights”: “that night of all nights”.

sentences.t: وَفِى ذٰلِكَ الْوَقْتِ كَانَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ جَالِسًا فِي دَسْتِ مَمْلَكَتِهِ وَبَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ أُمَرَاءُ دَوْلَتِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-fī dhālika al-waqti kāna al-maliku shahramānu jālisan fī dasti mamlakatihi wa-bayna yadayhi umarāʾu dawlatihi
sentences.l: And in that time King Shahramān was sitting on the seat of his kingdom, and between his hands the emirs of his state.
sentences.i: At that very hour King Shahramān was sitting on his throne, with the emirs of his realm before him.
sentences.n: Shahramān is Dunyā's father. dast, a Persian word, “seat of honour, throne”. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”: in his presence.

sentences.t: إِذْ دَخَلَ عَلَيْهِ عَرِيفُ الصُّيَّاغِ وَبِيَدِهِ حُقٌّ كَبِيرٌ فَقَدَّمَ وَفَتَحَهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيِ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: idh dakhala ʿalayhi ʿarīfu al-ṣuyyāghi wa-bi-yadihi ḥuqqun kabīrun fa-qaddama wa-fataḥahu bayna yadayi al-maliki
sentences.l: When there came in upon him the head of the goldsmiths, and in his hand a great casket, and he presented and opened it between the hands of the king.
sentences.i: In came the master of the goldsmiths' guild with a large casket in his hand, which he set before the king and opened.
sentences.n: ʿarīf, “headman, master of a guild”. ḥuqq, “a small box or casket”, often for jewels; the print marks its doubled qāf. fa-qaddama, “and he brought (it) forward”, is our reading of فقدم; qadima, “he came forward”, is also possible.

sentences.t: وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْهُ عُلْبَةً لَطِيفَةً تُسَاوِي مِائَةَ أَلْفِ دِينَارٍ لِمَا فِيهِ مِنَ الْجَوَاهِرِ وَالْيَوَاقِيتِ وَالزُّمُرُّدِ مِمَّا لَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ أَحَدٌ مِنْ مُلُوكِ الْأَقْطَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-akhraja minhu ʿulbatan laṭīfatan tusāwī miʾata alfi dīnārin li-mā fīhi mina al-jawāhiri wa-al-yawāqīti wa-al-zumurrudi mimmā lā yaqdiru ʿalayhi aḥadun min mulūki al-aqṭāri
sentences.l: And he brought out from it a fine little-box worth a hundred thousand dinars, for what was in it of the jewels and the rubies and the emerald, such as none of the kings of the regions could afford.
sentences.i: From it he took out a dainty little box worth a hundred thousand dinars for the jewels set in it, rubies and emeralds such as no king anywhere could buy.
sentences.n: li-mā fīhi, “for what is in it”: li- gives the reason for its worth. The pronoun of fīhi is masculine although ʿulba, “box”, is feminine, perhaps thinking of the ḥuqq; Middle Arabic is loose with such agreement. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to (obtain)”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا الْمَلِكُ تَعَجَّبَ مِنْ حُسْنِهَا وَالْتَفَتَ إِلَى الْخَادِمِ الْكَبِيرِ الَّذِى جَرَى لَهُ مَعَ الْعَجُوزِ مَاجَرَى
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā al-maliku taʿajjaba min ḥusnihā wa-iltafata ilā al-khādimi al-kabīri alladhī jarā lahu maʿa al-ʿajūzi mā jarā
sentences.l: And when the king saw it, he marvelled at its beauty, and turned to the great eunuch, the one to whom befell with the old woman what befell.
sentences.i: When the king saw it he marvelled at its beauty, and turned to the chief eunuch, the one who had had that encounter with the old woman.
sentences.n: al-khādim al-kabīr, “the great servant”: the chief eunuch, the same man who stopped the nurse at the gate. The print runs mā jarā together (ماجرى).

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ يَا كَافُورُ خُذْ هٰذِهِ الْعُلْبَةَ وَامْضِ بِهَا إِلَى السَّيِّدَةِ دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu yā kāfūru khudh hādhihi al-ʿulbata wa-imḍi bihā ilā al-sayyidati dunyā
sentences.l: And he said to him: O Kāfūr, take this box and go with it to the Lady Dunyā.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Kāfūr, take this box to the Lady Dunyā.”
sentences.n: Kāfūr, “camphor”, a name commonly given to black eunuchs. maḍā bi-, “to go off with, to take”: bi- of accompaniment.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهَا الْخَادِمُ وَمَضَى حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَي مَقْصُورَةِ بِنْتِ الْمَلِكِ فَوَجَدَ بَابَهَا مُغْلَقًا وَالْعَجُوزَ نَائِمَةً عَلَى عَتَبَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahā al-khādimu wa-maḍā ḥattā waṣala ilā maqṣūrati binti al-maliki fa-wajada bābahā mughlaqan wa-al-ʿajūza nāʾimatan ʿalā ʿatabatihi
sentences.l: And the eunuch took it and went until he reached the chamber of the king's daughter, and found its door locked and the old woman sleeping on its threshold.
sentences.i: The eunuch took it and went off until he came to the princess's apartment; he found the door locked and the old woman asleep on the threshold.
sentences.n: The print spells ilā with a final ي (الي).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَادِمُ إِلَى هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ وَأَنْتُمْ نَائِمُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khādimu ilā hādhihi al-sāʿati wa-antum nāʾimūna
sentences.l: And the eunuch said: Until this hour, and you (pl.) are sleeping?
sentences.i: The eunuch said, “Still asleep, at this hour?”

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتِ الْعَجُوزُ كَلَامَ الْخَادِمِ انْتَبَهَتْ مِنْ مَنَامِهَا وَخَافَتْ مِنْهُ وَقَالَتْ اصْبِرْ حَتَّى آتِيَكَ بِالْمِفْتَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿati al-ʿajūzu kalāma al-khādimi intabahat min manāmihā wa-khāfat minhu wa-qālat iṣbir ḥattā ātiyaka bi-al-miftāḥi
sentences.l: And when the old woman heard the speech of the eunuch, she woke from her sleep and was afraid of him, and said: Be patient until I bring you the key.
sentences.i: When the old woman heard the eunuch's voice she woke with a start, and was afraid of him, and said, “Wait while I fetch you the key.”
sentences.n: The print has سعمت, a misprint for samiʿat (سمعت), “she heard”, corrected here. atā bi-, “to come with”: “to bring”; the verb takes bi-.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَتْ عَلَى وَجْهِهَا هَارِبَةً
sentences.tr: thumma kharajat ʿalā wajhihā hāribatan
sentences.l: Then she went out on her face, fleeing.
sentences.i: Then she ran off, fleeing for her life.
sentences.n: kharaja ʿalā wajhihi, “to go out on one's face”: to go off headlong, with no thought of where.

sentences.t: هٰذَا مَاكَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِهَا
sentences.tr: hādhā mā kāna min amrihā
sentences.l: This is what was of her affair.
sentences.i: So much for her.
sentences.n: The print runs mā kāna together (ماكان).

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَا كَانَ مِنْ أَمْرِ الْخَادِمِ فَإِنَّهُ عَرَفَ أَنَّهَا مُرْتَابَةٌ فَخَلَعَ الْبَابَ وَدَخَلَ الْمَقْصُورَةَ فَوَجَدَ السَّيِّدَةَ دُنْيَا مُعَانِقَةً لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَهُمَا نَائِمَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā mā kāna min amri al-khādimi fa-innahu ʿarafa annahā murtābatun fa-khalaʿa al-bāba wa-dakhala al-maqṣūrata fa-wajada al-sayyidata dunyā muʿāniqatan li-tāji al-mulūki wa-humā nāʾimāni
sentences.l: And as for what was of the affair of the eunuch, he knew that she was suspect, so he wrenched-off the door and entered the chamber, and found the Lady Dunyā embracing Tāj al-Mulūk, and the two sleeping.
sentences.i: As for the eunuch, he saw that she had something to hide, so he forced the door and went in, and found the Lady Dunyā in Tāj al-Mulūk's arms, the two of them asleep.
sentences.n: murtāba, “in doubt, suspect”; here, with a guilty conscience. khalaʿa al-bāb, “to pull off the door”, that is, from its hinges. muʿāniqatan li-, “embracing”: li- marks the object of the participle.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَى ذٰلِكَ تَحَيَّرَ فِي أَمْرِهِ وَهَمَّ أَنْ يَعُودَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾā dhālika taḥayyara fī amrihi wa-hamma an yaʿūda ilā al-maliki
sentences.l: And when he saw that, he was bewildered in his affair, and was about to return to the king.
sentences.i: When he saw it he did not know what to do, and was on the point of going back to the king.
sentences.n: hamma an, “to be on the point of, to intend to”; the print marks its doubled mīm.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبَهَتِ السَّيِّدَةُ دُنْيَا فَوَجَدَتْهُ فَتَغَيَّرَتْ وَاصْفَرَّ لَوْنُهَا وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يَا كَافُورُ اسْتُرْ مَاسَتَرَ اللّٰهُ
sentences.tr: fa-intabahati al-sayyidatu dunyā fa-wajadathu fa-taghayyarat wa-iṣfarra lawnuhā wa-qālat lahu yā kāfūru ustur mā satara allāhu
sentences.l: And the Lady Dunyā woke and found him, and she changed and her colour went-yellow, and she said to him: O Kāfūr, cover what God has covered.
sentences.i: The Lady Dunyā woke and saw him there; her face changed and turned pale, and she said to him, “Kāfūr, hide what God has hidden.”
sentences.n: ustur mā satara allāh, “cover what God has covered”: a proverbial plea not to expose a fault that Providence has kept hidden. The print runs mā satara together (ماستر).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَنَا لَا أَقْدِرُ أَنْ أُخْفِيَ شَيْأً عَنِ الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla anā lā aqdiru an ukhfiya shayʾan ʿani al-maliki
sentences.l: And he said: I am not able to hide a thing from the king.
sentences.i: He said, “I cannot hide anything from the king.”
sentences.n: The print spells shayʾan as شيأ, an older spelling with the hamza on an alif.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَفَلَ الْبَابَ عَلَيْهِمَا وَرَجَعَ إِلَى الْمَلِكِ
sentences.tr: thumma qafala al-bāba ʿalayhimā wa-rajaʿa ilā al-maliki
sentences.l: Then he locked the door upon the two of them and returned to the king.
sentences.i: Then he locked the door on them and went back to the king.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ هَلْ أَعْطَيْتَ الْعُلْبَةَ لِسَيِّدَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku hal aʿṭayta al-ʿulbata li-sayyidatika
sentences.l: And the king said to him: Did you give the box to your lady?
sentences.i: The king said to him, “Did you give the box to your mistress?”
sentences.n: aʿṭā with li- for the one given to, a Middle Arabic habit; Classical Arabic says aʿṭāhā al-ʿulba.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْخَادِمُ خُذِ الْعُلْبَةَ مَاشِي وَأَنَا لَا أَقْدِرُ أَنْ أُخْفِيَ عَنْكَ شَيْأً اعْلَمْ أَنِّي رَأَيْتُ عِنْدَ السَّيِّدَةِ دُنْيَا شَابًّا جَمِيلًا نَائِمًا مَعَهَا فِي فَرْشٍ وَاحِدٍ وَهُمَا مُتَعَانِقَانِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-khādimu khudhi al-ʿulbata māshī wa-anā lā aqdiru an ukhfiya ʿanka shayʾan iʿlam annī raʾaytu ʿinda al-sayyidati dunyā shābban jamīlan nāʾiman maʿahā fī farshin wāḥidin wa-humā mutaʿāniqāni
sentences.l: And the eunuch said to him: Take the box — nothing doing! And I am not able to hide from you a thing: know that I saw with the Lady Dunyā a handsome youth, sleeping with her in one bed, and the two embracing.
sentences.i: The eunuch said, “Here, take the box back — it never got there. I cannot keep anything from you: I tell you, I found a handsome young man in the Lady Dunyā's room, asleep with her in the same bed, the two of them in each other's arms.”
sentences.n: māshī is not clear to us. It may be mā shī, “(there is) nothing”, in the spoken form of mā shayʾ, “the errand came to nothing”; or the colloquial māshī, “all right, very well”. Either way he hands the box back undelivered. The print spells shayʾan as شيأ. farsh, “bedding”, here the bed.

sentences.t: فَأَمَرَ الْمَلِكُ بِإِحْضَارِهِمَا فَلَمَّا حَضَرَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ قَالَ لَهُمَا مَا هٰذَا الْفِعَالُ وَاشْتَدَّ بِهِ الْغَيْظُ
sentences.tr: fa-amara al-maliku bi-iḥḍārihimā fa-lammā ḥaḍarā bayna yadayhi qāla lahumā mā hādhā al-fiʿālu wa-ishtadda bihi al-ghayẓu
sentences.l: And the king commanded the bringing of the two of them; and when they were present between his hands, he said to them: What is this doing? And the rage grew-hard upon him.
sentences.i: The king had them both brought, and when they stood before him he said to them, “What is this you have done?” and his fury mounted.
sentences.n: amara bi-, “to order (a thing)”: the verb takes bi-. fiʿāl, “deeds, doings”, here with a note of reproach.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَ قَمْشَةً وَهَمَّ أَنْ يَضْرِبَ تَاجَ الْمُلُوكِ فَرَمَتِ السَّيِّدَةُ دُنْيَا وَجْهَهَا عَلَيْهِ وَقَالَتْ لِأَبِيهَا اقْتُلْنِي قَبْلَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadha qamshatan wa-hamma an yaḍriba tāja al-mulūki fa-ramati al-sayyidatu dunyā wajhahā ʿalayhi wa-qālat li-abīhā uqtulnī qablahu
sentences.l: And he took a whip and was about to strike Tāj al-Mulūk, and the Lady Dunyā threw her face upon him and said to her father: Kill me before him.
sentences.i: He seized a whip and was about to strike Tāj al-Mulūk, but the Lady Dunyā threw herself on him and said to her father, “Kill me first.”
sentences.n: qamsha, “whip”, a Turkish word (qamchı) in the Arabic of the later period; we are not certain of its vowels. ramat wajhahā ʿalayhi, “she threw her face on him”: she flung herself over him to shield him. The print marks the doubled mīm of hamma.

sentences.t: فَنَهَرَهَا الْمَلِكُ وَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يَمْضُوا بِهَا إِلَى حُجْرَتِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-naharahā al-maliku wa-amarahum an yamḍū bihā ilā ḥujratihā
sentences.l: And the king rebuked her, and commanded them that they go with her to her room.
sentences.i: The king shouted her down and ordered his people to take her off to her room.
sentences.n: maḍā bi-, “to take (someone) away”: bi- of accompaniment.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتَ إِلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ وَقَالَ لَهُ وَيْلَكَ مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ وَمَنْ أَبُوكَ وَمَاجَسَّرَكَ عَلَى ابْنَتِي
sentences.tr: thumma iltafata ilā tāji al-mulūki wa-qāla lahu waylaka min ayna anta wa-man abūka wa-mā jassaraka ʿalā ibnatī
sentences.l: Then he turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and said to him: Woe to you! From where are you, and who is your father, and what made-you-bold against my daughter?
sentences.i: Then he turned to Tāj al-Mulūk and said, “Curse you! Where are you from, who is your father, and what gave you the nerve to touch my daughter?”
sentences.n: jassara ʿalā, “to embolden against”: mā jassaraka ʿalā, “what made you dare (to approach)”. The print runs mā jassaraka together (ماجسرك).

sentences.t: فَقَالَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ اعْلَمْ أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ أَنَّكَ إِنْ قَتَلْتَنِي هَلَكْتَ وَنَدِمْتَ أَنْتَ وَمَنْ فِي مَمْلَكَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla tāju al-mulūki iʿlam ayyuhā al-maliku annaka in qataltanī halakta wa-nadimta anta wa-man fī mamlakatika
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said: Know, O king, that if you kill me you will perish and repent, you and whoever is in your kingdom.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said, “Know, O king, that if you kill me, you will be ruined and sorry for it, you and everyone in your kingdom.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ وَلِمَ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku wa-lima dhālika
sentences.l: And the king said to him: And why that?
sentences.i: The king said, “And why so?”
sentences.n: The print itself points wa-lima, “and why”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ اعْلَمْ أَنِّي ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ سُلَيْمَانَ شَاهْ وَمَا تَدْرِي إِلَّا وَهُوَ قَدْ أَقْبَلَ عَلَيْكَ بِخَيْلِهِ وَرَجِلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla iʿlam annī ibnu al-maliki sulaymāna shāh wa-mā tadrī illā wa-huwa qad aqbala ʿalayka bi-khaylihi wa-rajilihi
sentences.l: And he said: Know that I am the son of King Sulaymān Shāh; and you will not know but that he has come upon you with his horse and his foot.
sentences.i: He said, “Know that I am the son of King Sulaymān Shāh; and before you know it he will be upon you with his horsemen and his foot-soldiers.”
sentences.n: mā tadrī illā wa-, “you will not know (anything) but that …”: “before you know it”. bi-khaylihi wa-rajilihi, “with his horse and his foot”: with all his cavalry and infantry, a Qurʾānic pair. The print marks the doubled lām of illā.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْمَلِكُ شَهْرَمَانُ ذٰلِكَ الْكَلَامَ أَرَادَ أَنْ يُؤَخِّرَ قَتْلَهُ وَيَضَعَهُ فِى السِّجْنِ حَتَّى يَنْظُرَ صِحَّةَ قَوْلِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-maliku shahramānu dhālika al-kalāma arāda an yuʾakhkhira qatlahu wa-yaḍaʿahu fī al-sijni ḥattā yanẓura ṣiḥḥata qawlihi
sentences.l: And when King Shahramān heard that speech, he wanted to delay his killing and put him in the prison until he should look into the truth of his saying.
sentences.i: When King Shahramān heard this he was minded to put off killing him and keep him in prison until he could see whether he was telling the truth.
sentences.n: The print marks the doubled khāʾ of yuʾakhkhira.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ وَزِيرُهُ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ الرَّأْيُ عِنْدِي أَنْ تُعَجِّلَ قَتْلَ هٰذَا الْعِلْقِ فَإِنَّهُ تَجَاسَرَ عَلَى بَنَاتِ الْمُلُوكِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu wazīruhu yā malika al-zamāni al-raʾyu ʿindī an tuʿajjila qatla hādhā al-ʿilqi fa-innahu tajāsara ʿalā banāti al-mulūki
sentences.l: And his vizier said to him: O king of the age, the opinion with me is that you hasten the killing of this ʿilq, for he has dared against the daughters of the kings.
sentences.i: But his vizier said to him, “King of the age, my advice is to put this wretch to death at once, for he has dared to lay hands on the daughters of kings.”
sentences.n: ʿilq is properly “a precious thing”; in the speech of the period it is also a coarse insult for a man, “catamite”, and that is how the vizier uses it. tajāsara ʿalā, “to make bold against, to presume upon”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِلسَّيَّافِ اضْرِبْ عُنُقَهُ فَإِنَّهُ خَائِنٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla li-al-sayyāfi iḍrib ʿunuqahu fa-innahu khāʾinun
sentences.l: And he said to the swordsman: Strike his neck, for he is a traitor.
sentences.i: So the king said to the executioner, “Cut off his head; he is a traitor.”
sentences.n: sayyāf, “swordsman”, the executioner; the print marks the doubled yāʾ. ḍaraba ʿunuqahu, “to strike his neck”: to behead.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَهُ السَّيَّافُ وَشَدَّ وِثَاقَهُ وَرَفَعَ يَدَهُ وَشَاوَرَ الْأُمَرَاءَ أَوَّلًا وَثَانِيًا وَقَصَدَ بِذٰلِكَ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِى الْأَمْرِ تَوَانٍ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhahu al-sayyāfu wa-shadda wathāqahu wa-rafaʿa yadahu wa-shāwara al-umarāʾa awwalan wa-thāniyan wa-qaṣada bi-dhālika an yakūna fī al-amri tawānin
sentences.l: And the swordsman took him and bound his bond tight and raised his hand, and consulted the emirs a first and a second (time), and he aimed by that that there be in the matter a delay.
sentences.i: The executioner took him, tied him fast and raised his arm; then he looked to the emirs once, and twice, meaning to gain some delay in the business.
sentences.n: shāwara, “to consult”: the executioner, by custom, asks leave before the stroke, and here asks again to give time for a reprieve. tawānin, “slackness, delay”. The print marks the doubled letters of shadda and awwalan.

sentences.t: فَزَعَقَ عَلَيْهِ الْمَلِكُ وَقَالَ لَهُ إِلَى مَتَى تُشَاوِرُ إِنْ شَاوَرْتَ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى ضَرَبْتُ عُنُقَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-zaʿaqa ʿalayhi al-maliku wa-qāla lahu ilā matā tushāwiru in shāwarta marratan ukhrā ḍarabtu ʿunuqaka
sentences.l: And the king shouted at him and said to him: Until when will you consult? If you consult another time, I shall strike your neck.
sentences.i: The king roared at him, “How long are you going to keep asking? Ask once more and I will strike off your own head!”

sentences.t: فَرَفَعَ السَّيَّافُ يَدَهُ حَتَّى بَانَ شَعْرُإِبْطِهِ وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَضْرِبَ عُنُقَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-rafaʿa al-sayyāfu yadahu ḥattā bāna shaʿru ibṭihi wa-arāda an yaḍriba ʿunuqahu
sentences.l: So the swordsman raised his hand till the hair of his armpit showed, and wanted to strike his neck.
sentences.i: So the executioner raised his arm so high that the hair of his armpit showed, and was about to strike off his head;
sentences.n: “Until the hair of his armpit showed”: a stock phrase of the Nights for the executioner's arm raised to the full for the stroke. The print runs shaʿr ibṭihi together (شعرابطه).

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
